# Beyond 0

Beyond 0 is a project focused on understanding how Earth's climate has changed over time and what we can learn from historical climate data. I developed it as an interactive platform that brings climate data, statistical analysis, and visualization together in one place.

The project uses historical observations to explore long-term climate trends, examine differences across geographical regions, and study how these patterns develop over the years. It also includes statistical models to explore possible future trends, with their performance tested against data they were not trained on.

One of the main goals of Beyond 0 is to make climate data easier to explore and understand. Instead of presenting users with large datasets and complicated numbers, the platform provides visual tools and clear analysis that help reveal patterns and make the information more accessible.

I believe understanding climate change starts with understanding the data behind it. Beyond 0 is my attempt to make that process more accessible and encourage people to explore the science for themselves.
details:
Beyond 0 – Exploring Earth's Changing Temperature

What does the project do?

Beyond 0 is a project I built to explore how Earth's temperature has changed over the past decades using real data from NASA.

I wanted to do more than just show a graph saying that the planet is getting warmer. I wanted to understand what is actually happening, how temperature changes from one region to another, and what the data might tell us about the coming years.

The project takes NASA's MERRA-2 temperature data and turns it into an interactive website where people can explore historical changes, compare different regions, and see the results of statistical analysis and forecasting.

How does it work?

I used NASA's MERRA-2 dataset, specifically the T2M variable, which represents air temperature at 2 meters above the surface.

The dataset contains monthly observations from January 1980 to August 2026. I processed the data using Python, converted temperatures from Kelvin to Celsius, and used 1981–2010 as the reference period for calculating temperature anomalies.

After preparing the data, I worked on several parts:

  • Historical analysis: Studying how global temperatures have changed over time.
  • Trend analysis: Using linear regression and Theil–Sen estimation to measure long-term temperature trends.
  • Statistical testing: Checking which temperature trends are statistically significant and examining the reliability of the results.
  • Spatial analysis: Looking at temperature changes across a global grid of 361 × 576 cells.
  • Forecasting: Using autoregressive time-series models and comparing machine-learning approaches to explore possible future temperature patterns.
  • Visualization: Bringing the results together in an interactive website so users can explore the findings without having to work with raw scientific data.

What are the benefits?

One of the biggest problems with scientific datasets is that they are not always easy for everyone to understand or use.

Beyond 0 tries to make that easier. Instead of asking users to download large files and process them themselves, the project presents the results in a more accessible way.

It can help students learn about climate change, allow curious users to explore real NASA data, and give people a better understanding of how temperature changes across different parts of the world.

It also shows how programming and data science can be used to study real environmental problems.

What is the intended impact?

My main goal is to make climate data easier to explore and understand.

I hope Beyond 0 encourages more people, especially students, to work with scientific data and become interested in climate science. I also wanted to show that you do not need a large research team or expensive equipment to start building something useful with open NASA data.

The project is an educational and analytical tool, not a replacement for professional climate models. Its forecasts are based on historical patterns and should be understood as estimates, not guaranteed predictions.

What tools and technologies did I use?

I developed Beyond 0 entirely as a software project.

  • Python: Data processing and scientific calculations.
  • NumPy: Numerical operations and working with large datasets.
  • Next.js and React: Building the website and its interactive interface.
  • TypeScript: Writing the frontend logic.
  • Tailwind CSS and CSS: Designing the interface.
  • JSON and binary files: Storing and delivering processed data efficiently.
  • API routes: Connecting the analytical data with the website.
  • Git and GitHub: Managing the source code and project versions.
  • Visual Studio Code and Node.js: Development environment and application tools.

The project uses NASA MERRA-2 data from NASA's GES DISC. No specialized physical hardware was required.

What makes the project creative?

What makes Beyond 0 interesting to me is that it combines several things I enjoy working with: programming, mathematics, statistics, and science.

I did not want to create another website with a few temperature charts. I wanted to build something where different types of analysis work together.

For example, a user can look at the historical temperature trend, explore where the changes are happening geographically, and then examine statistical results and short-term forecasts.

I also had to think about performance. The spatial dataset contains more than 200,000 grid cells, so I used preprocessed data and binary files to avoid sending unnecessarily large amounts of data to the browser.

What factors did I consider?

During development, I had to consider several things:

  • Data quality: Making sure the data was processed consistently and that temperature conversions were correct.
  • Scientific accuracy: Using established statistical methods instead of relying on a single calculation.
  • Uncertainty: Understanding that statistical results and forecasts have limitations.
  • Performance: Making the website capable of handling large datasets without becoming unnecessarily slow.
  • Usability: Presenting scientific information in a way that people without a technical background can understand.
  • Future development: Building the project so that more datasets and analysis methods can be added later.

Final thoughts

Beyond 0 started with a simple question: How much can we learn about our changing planet if we take real scientific data and actually work with it?

Building it gave me the chance to combine what I have learned about programming, mathematics, and data analysis into one project. It was also a challenge because I had to deal with large datasets, scientific calculations, and web development at the same time.

I hope the result makes exploring Earth's temperature changes a little easier and inspires other students to use technology to investigate problems that matter.
